context.heading: A title, not a name
context.body: The speaker calls himself qoheleth ("the Teacher"), a word related to qahal, the assembly of God's people. It pictures someone who gathers a congregation and speaks to it. The odd grammatical form suggests a role or pen name. That is part of why readers differ on whether Solomon wrote the book or a later sage wrote in his voice.

context.heading: Chasing the wind
context.body: Re'ut ruach ("pursuit of the wind") is the Teacher's second refrain. You can run after wind all day and close your hand on nothing. The phrase does not say effort is evil; it says effort cannot capture what we most want from it.

context.heading: Under the sun
context.body: The phrase "under the sun" appears about 29 times and is found nowhere else in the Old Testament. It marks the Teacher's vantage point: life observed from ground level, inside the endless cycles of sun, wind and streams (vv. 5–7). He is not denying God, but testing what can be known by looking only at the world.

theology.title: God made a world of rhythm
theology.body: The circuits of sun, wind and water (vv. 5–7) feel tedious to the Teacher, yet they reflect God's faithful ordering of creation (Genesis 8:22). What is wearying to us is reliable because of Him. The book starts by naming our frustration honestly before pointing to the God behind the cycles.

theology.title: Futility is not the last word
theology.body: Paul seems to draw on this book when he writes that creation was subjected to futility (Romans 8:20). The Greek Old Testament used the same word, mataiotes, to render hevel. Paul adds what the Teacher could only long for: creation will be set free when God's children are revealed.

application.title: Nothing new on your feed
application.body: The Teacher says the eye is never satisfied with seeing (v. 8). An endless scroll promises something new and delivers more of the same.
application.question: What are you hoping your next hour of scrolling will give you that it never has?

application.title: Forgotten by the next generation
application.body: Verse 11 says no one remembers earlier generations, and later ones will not remember us. That stings if our worth depends on legacy.
application.question: Which part of your work would still feel worth doing if no one ever remembered you did it?

context.heading: Nothing better
context.body: Verse 24 says there is nothing tov ("better") than to eat, drink and find satisfaction in work. Tov is the word God speaks over creation in Genesis 1. The Teacher is not recommending a party lifestyle. He is saying the ordinary goods of creation are real, but only when received from God rather than squeezed for meaning.

context.heading: A mind that will not rest
context.body: Verse 23 says the worker's days are full of pain and his task is ka'as ("vexation"), grief mixed with irritation. Even at night his mind does not rest. The Teacher describes the burnout of someone who has achieved everything he set out to do and is still restless.

theology.title: Gifts, not achievements
theology.body: The king's list is full of "I": I built, I planted, I acquired (vv. 4–8). The chapter ends with God as the subject: He gives wisdom, knowledge and joy (v. 26). What the king could not build for himself, God gives. Jesus makes the same point about storing up treasure on earth (Luke 12:16–21).

theology.title: Wisdom is still better
theology.body: Even with death in view, the Teacher insists wisdom beats folly as light beats darkness (v. 13). Ecclesiastes is not nihilism. It refuses easy answers while holding onto moral order, a tension the rest of Scripture resolves in Christ, "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom" (Colossians 2:3).

application.title: The project that would finally satisfy
application.body: The king tried every upgrade: houses, gardens, music, staff. Each one delivered and still left a gap.
application.question: What purchase or achievement are you currently telling yourself will finally be enough?

application.title: Leaving it to someone else
application.body: The Teacher hates that his life's work will pass to someone who may be a fool (vv. 18–19). Parents, business owners and anyone who builds something feel this.
application.question: How would you work differently if you accepted now that you will not control what happens to it after you?

application.title: Taste your lunch
application.body: Verse 24 commends simply enjoying food and work as gifts. Many of us eat at a desk while thinking about the next task.
application.question: When did you last enjoy an ordinary meal slowly enough to thank God for it?

context.heading: One fate for people and animals
context.body: Verse 19 says humans and animals share one miqreh ("fate"): both die and return to dust (Genesis 3:19). The Teacher is speaking of what can be observed under the sun. From that vantage point no one can tell what happens next, and verse 21 asks exactly that question.

context.heading: Who knows about the spirit?
context.body: Ruach ("spirit" or "breath") is the life God breathes into His creatures (Genesis 2:7; Psalm 104:29–30). Verse 21 asks who can know whether the human spirit goes upward. It is an honest question, not a denial. Later the Teacher answers it in part: the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7).

theology.title: God owns the calendar
theology.body: Every season in verses 2–8 is set by God, not by us. "Whatever God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it" (v. 14). The point is not fatalism but trust: the One who sets the times is also the One who makes everything beautiful in its time.

theology.title: Judgment and the wider Bible
theology.body: The Teacher sees wickedness in the courts and trusts that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked (vv. 16–17). Read within the whole Bible, the uncertainty of verses 19–21 is not the final answer. Jesus' resurrection shows that human beings are not like animals that simply return to dust (1 Corinthians 15:20–22).

theology.title: Beautiful in its time
theology.body: Verse 11 says God makes everything beautiful in its time, though we cannot see the whole from beginning to end. He works on a scale longer than one lifetime. Galatians 4:4 uses the same idea of timing: "when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son."

application.title: Not your season
application.body: Verses 2–8 include weeping, tearing down and refraining. Some seasons are not what we would choose.
application.question: Which season are you in right now that you keep trying to rush past?

application.title: A time to be silent
application.body: There is a time to keep quiet and a time to speak (v. 7). Group chats, comment sections and family arguments reward the instant reply.
application.question: What conversation this week needs you to wait before you speak?

application.title: Eternity in a busy heart
application.body: God has set eternity in the human heart (v. 11), yet we fill every quiet minute with noise. The ache for something lasting is a signal, not a malfunction.
application.question: When you feel that ache for something more, what do you usually reach for to quiet it?

context.heading: Work fueled by envy
context.body: Verse 4 traces much hard work back to qin'ah ("envy"), the same word for jealousy or rivalry. The Teacher sees that skill and labor often spring from wanting what a neighbor has. Ambition can look like diligence while being driven by comparison.

context.heading: The poor but wise youth
context.body: The parable of verses 13–16 contrasts an old, foolish king with a poor yeled ("youth") who rises from prison to the throne. Joseph comes to mind, but the story may be a general parable. Its sting is in the ending: even the popular new king is forgotten by the next generation.

context.heading: Tears and no comfort
context.body: Verse 1 opens with the tears of the oppressed and power in the hands of their oppressors. The Teacher even calls the dead and the unborn better off (vv. 2–3). It is the language of lament, voiced honestly, not a recommendation, and it shows how heavy injustice felt to him.

theology.title: God sees the oppressed
theology.body: The Teacher says twice that the oppressed have "no comforter" (v. 1). Scripture does not leave that verdict standing. God calls Himself the one who comforts His people (Isaiah 51:12), and Jesus sends the Spirit as the Comforter who stays (John 14:16).

theology.title: Made for company
theology.body: The praise of two over one echoes Genesis 2:18: it is not good for man to be alone. God made people for partnership and mutual help. The church takes up this pattern, a body where members carry one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2).

application.title: Two handfuls
application.body: Verse 6 says one handful with quiet is better than two handfuls with toil and chasing wind. Overtime, side gigs and constant upgrades can steal the very rest they promise.
application.question: What would you have to give up to live on one handful with quiet?

application.title: Who would pick you up?
application.body: Verse 10 pities the person who falls with no one to help them up. Many adults have work friends and online followers but no one who would show up.
application.question: Who would you call at 2 a.m., and who would call you?

application.title: Working for whom?
application.body: The man in verse 8 works endlessly with no one to share it, and never asks why. Many careers run on autopilot like that.
application.question: For whom are you depriving yourself of rest right now?

context.heading: Draw near to listen
context.body: Verse 1 says to approach God's house to shama ("listen"), a word that also means to heed or obey. Israel's central prayer begins "Hear, O Israel" (Deuteronomy 6:4). The Teacher contrasts this with the "sacrifice of fools," who offer rituals and words without listening at all.

context.heading: Officials watching officials
context.body: Verse 8 describes a medinah ("province") where each official is watched by a higher one. The word was used for administrative districts of large empires. The Teacher's point is sobering: layered bureaucracy can explain why justice is perverted without making it any better.

context.heading: Fools in the temple
context.body: The "sacrifice of fools" (v. 1) was worship offered without attention or obedience. The prophets condemned the same thing: offerings brought by people whose lives ignored God (Isaiah 1:11–17; 1 Samuel 15:22). The Teacher's point is that God wants hearing before He wants gifts.

theology.title: God is in heaven
theology.body: "God is in heaven and you are on earth, so let your words be few" (v. 2). Reverence is not distance for its own sake; it is accuracy about who God is. Jesus echoes this when He warns against heaping up empty phrases in prayer (Matthew 6:7).

theology.title: The power to enjoy is a gift
theology.body: Verse 19 says God gives wealth and also gives the ability to enjoy it. Those are two different gifts. Paul writes something similar: God richly provides everything for us to enjoy, so the rich should not trust in uncertain riches (1 Timothy 6:17).

application.title: Promises at church
application.body: Vows in the heat of a moment, a worship song, a crisis, are easy to make and easy to forget (vv. 4–5). The Teacher says that is worse than never promising.
application.question: What did you once promise God that you have quietly let slide?

application.title: More income, more mouths
application.body: "As goods increase, so do those who consume them" (v. 11). A raise rarely brings the peace we imagined because spending, worry and obligations rise with it.
application.question: What would change if you treated your next raise as a test of contentment rather than a solution?

application.title: Sleep of the worker
application.body: The laborer sleeps well, but the rich man's abundance keeps him awake (v. 12). Money worries look different at every income level.
application.question: What is keeping you awake that more money would not actually fix?

context.heading: An appetite never filled
context.body: Verse 7 says all a person's labor is for the mouth, yet the nephesh ("appetite") is never filled. Nephesh means throat, desire and life itself. The Teacher pictures a hunger deeper than the stomach that keeps asking for more.

context.heading: A strange kind of poverty
context.body: Verse 2 describes a man with riches, wealth and honor, lacking nothing his heart desires, yet unable to enjoy any of it while a stranger does. The Teacher calls it a sickness. Ancient readers would have counted him the most blessed man in town.

context.heading: Already named
context.body: Verse 10 says what exists was named long ago, and a person cannot contend with one stronger. The stronger one is God. In the ancient world, to name something was to define it, so the Teacher reminds us that humans are creatures whose nature has been set by their Maker.

theology.title: God names reality
theology.body: "Whatever exists has already been named" (v. 10). In Genesis, naming expresses authority. God has already defined what humans are, and no one can argue Him into a different verdict. Our limits are not an accident but part of being creatures.

theology.title: Who knows what is good?
theology.body: The chapter ends asking who knows what is good for a person in their fleeting life (v. 12). The Teacher leaves it open. Scripture answers that God has told us what is good (Micah 6:8), and that the life worth having is found in knowing Him (John 17:3).

application.title: Better than wandering desire
application.body: Verse 9 says what the eyes see is better than the wandering of desire. Online carts, home tours and the next phone model train us to live in imagined futures.
application.question: What do you already have that you have not enjoyed because your desire has wandered elsewhere?

application.title: A hundred children and no joy
application.body: The Teacher imagines the most outwardly successful life possible and still calls it empty without contentment (v. 3). Success on paper does not guarantee a good life.
application.question: Which mark of success are you chasing that would not fix the dissatisfaction underneath?

application.title: Many words, little meaning
application.body: "The more words, the more futility" (v. 11). Arguing with God, or with people online, rarely produces the clarity we want.
application.question: Which argument are you having, with God or anyone else, where more words are only adding fog?

context.heading: The house of mourning
context.body: Verse 2 prefers the house of evel ("mourning") to the house of feasting. Israelite mourning lasted days, with neighbors sitting with the family (Genesis 50:10). The Teacher says a funeral teaches the living something a party cannot: "death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart."

context.heading: No one who never sins
context.body: "There is not a righteous man on earth who always does good and never sins" (v. 20). Tsaddiq ("righteous") describes someone in right standing who lives faithfully. Even such a person is not sinless. Paul gathers the same conviction from the Psalms in Romans 3:10–12.

context.heading: A hard line to read
context.body: Verses 26–28 speak harshly of a seductive woman and say the Teacher found one upright man in a thousand, but not one woman. Many read this as a warning about the adulteress of Proverbs 7 and as one man's bitter tally, not God's verdict on women. Verse 29 then puts all humanity in the same place: God made people upright, and they all went looking for schemes.

theology.title: God made both days
theology.body: "In the day of prosperity be joyful, but in the day of adversity consider: God has made one as well as the other" (v. 14). Good and hard days are both under His hand. This is not a claim that God delights in pain, but that no season is outside His rule (Romans 8:28).

theology.title: Upright by design
theology.body: Verse 29 is a short commentary on Genesis 1–3. God created humanity good, and our crookedness came from our own inventions. The problem is not that we were made wrong but that we turned. That is why the remedy has to come from God, who in Christ makes a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17).

application.title: Don't ask about the good old days
application.body: Verse 10 calls it unwise to ask why former days were better than these. Nostalgia for a past church, decade or job can keep us from faithfulness now.
application.question: What 'better days' are you comparing your present to, and what is that comparison costing you?

application.title: Don't overhear everything
application.body: Verses 21–22 advise not taking every overheard comment to heart, since you have also cursed others. Screenshots and forwarded texts make this harder than ever.
application.question: Which comment about you are you still replaying that you would be wiser to let go?

application.title: Patience over pride
application.body: The patient spirit is better than the proud (v. 8). Pride wants to win the argument now; patience waits for the end of the matter.
application.question: Where is pride pushing you to settle something today that would be better settled later?

context.heading: Delayed sentences
context.body: Verse 11 notes that when a pitgam ("sentence") against an evil deed is not carried out quickly, people's hearts fill with schemes to do wrong. Pitgam is a Persian loanword for an official decree. The Teacher sees that slow justice teaches people they can get away with things.

context.heading: Wisdom you cannot find
context.body: Verse 17 uses matsa ("find" or "comprehend") three times: no one can find out the work God does under the sun. The wise may claim to know it, but cannot truly find it. Even the wisest observer meets a horizon.

context.heading: The face that shines
context.body: Verse 1 says wisdom makes a person's face shine and softens its hardness. In Hebrew, paneh ("face") stands for a person's whole presence. Wisdom changes not only what someone knows but how they carry themselves and how others experience them.

theology.title: It will go well for those who fear God
theology.body: The Teacher has seen the wicked live long, yet he says "I know it will be well with those who fear God" (v. 12). This is faith speaking against appearances, the same move Asaph makes in Psalm 73. Justice may be delayed, but it is not cancelled.

theology.title: God's work is bigger than our view
theology.body: Verse 17 is a humble admission that God's ways outrun human understanding, much like Isaiah 55:8–9. Paul echoes it in praise: "How unsearchable are His judgments" (Romans 11:33). The proper response to mystery is not despair but worship.

application.title: When cheaters win
application.body: The Teacher sees the wicked praised in the city where they did evil (v. 10). Coworkers who cut corners get promoted; people who game the system seem to prosper.
application.question: How do you keep doing right when you can see wrongdoing pay off around you?

application.title: Joy is commended, not merely allowed
application.body: Verse 15 says the Teacher commends joy. Some Christians treat enjoyment as suspicious, as if holiness meant grimness.
application.question: What good thing has God given you this week that you have been too guarded to enjoy?

application.title: Know when to speak
application.body: The wise heart knows the right time and procedure (v. 5). Raising a hard issue with a boss or spouse at the wrong moment can sink a good point.
application.question: What hard conversation do you need to have, and when is the wise time to have it?

context.heading: No work in Sheol
context.body: Verse 10 says there is no work, planning, knowledge or wisdom in she'ol ("Sheol"), the grave or realm of the dead. Much of the Old Testament pictures death this way, as silence and stillness (Psalm 6:5). The Teacher is speaking from under the sun, and the fuller hope of resurrection comes later in Scripture (Daniel 12:2; John 5:28–29).

context.heading: The dead know nothing
context.body: Verse 5 says the dead have no further reward and even their zekher ("memory") is forgotten. Read in context, the point is that the dead no longer share in life under the sun (v. 6). Read in the light of the whole Bible, it is not a full statement about what lies beyond death (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23).

theology.title: In the hand of God
theology.body: Verse 1 says the righteous and the wise and their deeds are "in the hand of God." No one knows whether love or hatred awaits them. The Teacher cannot read the future, but he can say whose hand holds it. Jesus says no one can snatch His sheep out of the Father's hand (John 10:29).

theology.title: Death defeated
theology.body: The Teacher sees one fate swallow everyone (vv. 2–3) and urges joy because life is short. The New Testament does not deny that verdict but overturns it: Christ shared our death so He might destroy the one who holds its power (Hebrews 2:14–15). Joy now becomes a foretaste, not a last meal.

application.title: Love your spouse in a fleeting life
application.body: Verse 9 says enjoy life with the wife you love all the days of your fleeting life. Busy seasons push a marriage to the margins, assuming there will be time later.
application.question: What would you do differently this week if you remembered that your days together are numbered?

application.title: Whatever your hand finds
application.body: Verse 10 urges doing your work with all your might. Half-hearted effort at a job we dislike is easy to justify.
application.question: Which task in front of you deserves your full effort even though no one is watching?

application.title: The forgotten wise man
application.body: A poor wise man saved a city, yet no one remembered him (v. 15). Wisdom often goes unthanked, and the loud voice gets the credit.
application.question: Whose quiet wisdom in your life have you overlooked because it came without a title?

context.heading: Wisdom sharpens the blade
context.body: Verse 10 says if the axe is dull, more strength is needed, but chokhmah ("wisdom") brings success. In Hebrew, wisdom often means practical skill, the word used for the craftsmen who built the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3). The Teacher praises working smarter, not only harder.

context.heading: A little bird will tell
context.body: Verse 20 warns not to curse the king even in your bedroom, because a bird of the air may carry your voice. Oph ("bird") here is a proverbial picture, like our saying "a little bird told me." Words spoken in private have a way of reaching the very person they are about.

theology.title: Order upended
theology.body: Verses 5–7 lament fools set in high places and slaves on horses while princes walk. The Teacher sees the world's order upside down. Scripture promises God will set it right, lifting the humble and bringing down the proud (Luke 1:52).

theology.title: The King over every throne
theology.body: Verses 16–17 contrast a land ruined by self indulgent rulers with one blessed by princes who govern for strength. Israel was taught that kings stood under God's law (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Behind every ruler, wise or foolish, stands the God who gives and removes kings (Daniel 2:21).

application.title: Sharpen before you swing
application.body: A dull axe takes more strength (v. 10). Many of us push harder instead of stopping to learn, plan or ask for help.
application.question: Where are you working harder at something when you should first be sharpening the blade?

application.title: The private complaint
application.body: Verse 20 warns that cursing a ruler in private still gets out. Texts, group chats and talk at home rarely stay where we put them.
application.question: What have you said about your boss, pastor or family member in private that you would not want them to hear?

application.title: One dead fly
application.body: A small folly ruins a reputation for wisdom (v. 1). One careless comment or one bad decision can undo years of trust.
application.question: What small habit could become the dead fly in an otherwise good reputation?

context.heading: You do not know the wind
context.body: Verse 5 says you do not know the path of the ruach ("wind" or "spirit") or how bones form in the womb. Jesus uses the same double sense of wind and Spirit to describe new birth (John 3:8). Our ignorance of how God works is not a reason to stop working.

context.heading: Sow in the morning and evening
context.body: Verse 6 urges sowing zera ("seed") in the morning and not holding back in the evening, since you do not know which will succeed. A farmer cannot wait for perfect conditions (v. 4) or nothing gets planted.

theology.title: Joy under judgment
theology.body: Verse 9 tells the young to rejoice and follow their heart, then adds that God will bring them into judgment for all of it. These are not opposites. Accountability to God is what keeps joy from becoming selfishness, and grace is what keeps accountability from becoming fear.

theology.title: The God who works all things
theology.body: "You do not know the work of God who makes everything" (v. 5). The Teacher points to God as Maker of all, including each child forming in the womb (Psalm 139:13–16). Our limited knowledge sits inside His complete knowledge.

application.title: Waiting for perfect conditions
application.body: "He who watches the wind will not sow" (v. 4). People delay giving, starting a family, changing careers or serving at church until everything lines up.
application.question: What good thing are you postponing until conditions are perfect?

application.title: Spread the risk
application.body: Verse 2 advises giving portions to seven, even eight, since you do not know what disaster may come. It is wisdom for money, friendships and service alike.
application.question: Where have you put all your hope in one basket that God never promised would hold?

application.title: Light is sweet
application.body: "Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun" (v. 7). The Teacher who began weary of the sun now delights in it, so joy in simple things can return.
application.question: What simple pleasure have you stopped noticing that you could deliberately enjoy this week?

context.heading: The silver cord snaps
context.body: Verse 6 piles up images of breaking: a silver cord snaps, a golden bowl is crushed, a pitcher shatters at the spring. Kesef ("silver") marks these as precious objects. Life is valuable and fragile at the same time, and once broken it cannot be mended by human hands.

context.heading: Dust and spirit
context.body: Verse 7 reverses Genesis 2:7: the aphar ("dust") returns to the ground, and the spirit returns to God who gave it. Here the Teacher answers part of his own question in 3:21. Human beings are more than dust because God gave them breath.

context.heading: The frame speaks
context.body: In verses 9–14 a narrator describes the Teacher as a careful sage who searched out and arranged proverbs. This frame gives the book's final verdict: "Fear God and keep His commandments" (v. 13). Readers differ on whether the frame corrects the Teacher or confirms what he was driving at all along, but both agree it is the last word.

theology.title: One Shepherd behind the words
theology.body: Verse 11 says the words of the wise are given by one Shepherd. Israel's God is the Shepherd of His people (Psalm 80:1), and Jesus calls Himself the Good Shepherd (John 10:11). The book that sounds the most human is still God's word, given to prod and steady us.

theology.title: Every deed into judgment
theology.body: The book ends with judgment: God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing (v. 14). That is what makes life under the sun matter after all. Paul makes the same claim, that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).

application.title: Remember while you are young
application.body: Verse 1 urges remembering your Creator before the years when you say, "I find no pleasure in them." Many people assume faith can wait until after school, after kids, after retirement.
application.question: What would it look like to take God seriously in the season you are in right now?

application.title: Too many books
application.body: "Of making many books there is no end, and much study wearies the body" (v. 12). Endless podcasts, articles and opinions can keep us learning without ever obeying.
application.question: Which truth do you already know well enough that you need to act on it instead of reading more about it?

application.title: The whole duty
application.body: Fear God and keep His commandments (v. 13). After twelve chapters of questions, the answer is simple to say and hard to live.
application.question: Where in your week is it hardest to let the fear of God, not the fear of people, decide what you do?
